The Wegovy Backed Me Up. MiraLax, Fiber, a $600 Script - None Fixed Why.

I'm a nurse. 38 years. So when the constipation from my Wegovy got bad, I tried to fix it the way I'd fix anything. One careful step at a time.

MiraLax first. Then the fiber powder everyone swears by, that gritty sludge you choke down twice a day. When those stopped touching it, my own doctor slid a $600-a-month script for Linzess across the desk like it settled things.

Here's the part nobody tells you. Every one of those options was built to force something out. Not one fixed why my gut had quit in the first place. And each came with its own misery. I'd watched Linzess patients so scared of the diarrhea they couldn't be 30 seconds from a bathroom. One took time off work over it.

I didn't want a chemical evacuation on a timer. I wanted my own body working again, the way it had my whole life.

Quitting the shot was never on the table. Go off it and the weight comes back. I'd watched too many patients do exactly that. Square one.

So I stayed backed up. Seven, eight, nine days of nothing. Bloated like I'd swallowed rocks, and scared of where it was heading.

I've been a nurse too long to chase every fix that gets passed around online. I'd about made my peace that this was just my life now.

Then about two months ago, one of my regular patients came in for her appointment. Sweet lady on Mounjaro for the past few months. She'd been struggling with constipation the entire time - two months of living off laxatives, miserable.

But this time she seemed different. More relaxed somehow.

I asked her how she was managing, and she said something I didn't expect. She told me she was actually going regularly now. She'd found this tea - oolong tea - with natural antioxidants and gentle caffeine. Been drinking it every morning. And for the first time in months, she was having normal bowel movements. No cramping. No laxatives. No fear.

I'll be honest, I was very skeptical. I've heard every miracle cure story you can imagine. But she seemed so genuinely relieved. Like she'd finally found something that actually worked.

That same night, I was on day 8 without a bowel movement. My stomach was so distended I couldn't sleep comfortably. I laid there feeling bloated and genuinely scared. And I kept thinking about what she'd said. So I looked it up.

Turns out, the antioxidants in oolong tea - along with natural caffeine and L-theanine - support digestive motility and gut microbiome health naturally. It doesn't force contractions like stimulant laxatives do. Plus it hydrates you and activates your body's natural gastrocolic reflex. The science actually made sense.

I ordered some. Figured I had nothing to lose. Worst case, it wouldn't work and I'd be out a few dollars.

When it arrived, I made a cup that first morning. I didn't expect much. Just another thing to try.

After about a week, things started moving a little. From once a week to every 4-5 days. Better. But not life-changing.

So I ordered a different brand. This one was cheaper, came in tea bags instead of loose leaf. After two weeks, things stayed about the same. Maybe every 3-4 days. Still too uncomfortable.

I was getting frustrated. Everyone said oolong tea worked. But it wasn't working for me.

So I went back and started reading more carefully. That's when I noticed something. People weren't just saying "oolong tea." They were getting specific about which oolong tea.

One person said they tried three different brands before finding one that actually worked. Another mentioned most oolong tea you can buy online is "tea dust" - the broken leftover scraps from processing that don't have any of the actual healing compounds.

I started researching. Turns out, most oolong teas are:

\- Over-processed (which destroys the polyphenols)

\- Grown at low elevations (weaker potency)

\- Mixed with tea dust and fillers

\- Sprayed with pesticides

\- Machine-harvested (damages the leaves)

The oolong teas that actually worked for digestive support had to be:

\- Whole leaf (not dust or broken pieces)

\- Grown above 4,500 feet (higher altitude = more potent polyphenols)

\- Hand-picked at peak harvest (preserves the catechins and L-theanine)

\- Traditionally processed (protects the healing compounds)

\- Organic (no pesticides blocking absorption)

I kept seeing the same brand mentioned over and over in the reviews and testimonials. PiPi Tea.

I ordered it. It was more expensive than the others I'd tried, but at that point I didn't care.

When it arrived, I could tell the difference immediately. The leaves were whole, tightly rolled, and perfectly oxidized. The smell was different - richer, almost floral. When I steeped it, the color was deeper.

I made a cup that first morning. Steeped it for five minutes. I didn't expect much. I'd already tried two other brands.

But about 30 minutes later, I noticed something. The usual morning bloat wasn't building up. Like someone had activated my digestive system again. I went from feeling that constant pressure in my abdomen to actually feeling movement - gentle, natural movement. I could actually feel the gastrocolic reflex working like it should for the first time in months.

That night, I had my first normal bowel movement in over a week. Actually normal - no straining. No cramping. No sitting there for 30 minutes with nothing happening. Just... normal.

When I woke up the next morning, I laid there stunned. The bloated feeling was gone. I'd slept through the night without that rock-in-my-stomach feeling for the first time in months.

By the end of the first week, I was going every single day. Every day. Not every 4-5 days like with the other brands. Every single morning like clockwork. I tracked it for three days straight because I didn't believe it. It hadn't been regular in months.

That bloated feeling that made me afraid to eat? Gone. The straining for hours with nothing happening? Cleared up almost completely. I could work a full shift without feeling backed up and uncomfortable.

It's been two months now. I go every single morning. Every morning. The bloating is gone. The fear is gone. Sometimes I skip a day after a really stressful shift when I'm not drinking enough water, but it's nothing. Nothing compared to what it was.

I saw my patient last week and thanked her. She just smiled and said she was glad it helped.

I Refused to Quit My GLP-1. Here's How I Finally Solved the Constipation

I've been a nurse for 38 years, and GLP-1 constipation is one of the hardest side effects I see patients struggle with. The bloating that makes them feel like a balloon. The backed-up feeling when nothing's moving through. That fear of eating because everything just... stopped. I've had patients tell me they go 7, 8, 9 days without a bowel movement. Day and night, they feel stuck.

About three years ago, it happened to me. I started Wegovy for weight management. Like my patients, I thought the constipation would be manageable. I was wrong. All those years of telling patients "just drink more water and eat fiber" — I learned firsthand how useless that advice is when you're on a GLP-1.

At first it was just going every 2-3 days instead of daily. Then came the bloating. That constant pressure in my abdomen that made me feel like I'd swallowed rocks. By the end of my shift, I could feel the backup getting worse. But the worst part? The fear. The fear of eating because I was tracking mentally how much I'd eaten that hadn't come out yet. I'd wake up on day 7 of no movement feeling genuinely scared. Would I have to go to the ER? The straining. The hours on the toilet with nothing happening. The hemorrhoids. I Refused to Quit My GLP-1. Here's How I Finally Solved the Constipation

I've been a nurse for 38 years, and GLP-1 constipation is one of the hardest side effects I see patients struggle with. The bloating that makes them feel like a balloon. The backed-up feeling when nothing's moving through. That fear of eating because everything just... stopped. I've had patients tell me they go 7, 8, 9 days without a bowel movement. Day and night, they feel stuck.

About three years ago, it happened to me. I started Wegovy for weight management. Like my patients, I thought the constipation would be manageable. I was wrong. All those years of telling patients "just drink more water and eat fiber" — I learned firsthand how useless that advice is when you're on a GLP-1.

At first it was just going every 2-3 days instead of daily. Then came the bloating. That constant pressure in my abdomen that made me feel like I'd swallowed rocks. By the end of my shift, I could feel the backup getting worse. But the worst part? The fear. The fear of eating because I was tracking mentally how much I'd eaten that hadn't come out yet. I'd wake up on day 7 of no movement feeling genuinely scared. Would I have to go to the ER? The straining. The hours on the toilet with nothing happening. The hemorrhoids. I was exhausted, uncomfortable, and miserable no matter what I tried.

Now I was the one living with it. And let me tell you, every patient was right. It's a living hell.

My doctor suggested I could try Linzess. $600 a month for prescription-strength relief. Or maybe I should just stop the Wegovy entirely. I smiled politely. But I knew I wasn't going to do either. I'd seen too many patients quit their GLP-1 and regain all the weight — back to square one. And the ones on Linzess? The diarrhea was so severe and unpredictable they were afraid to leave home. One patient told me she had to take time off work because she couldn't be more than 30 seconds from a bathroom. For $600 a month. And for what? Most of them said it worked great at first, then their body got used to it and it stopped being effective.

I asked him if there was anything else. Anything besides a $600 prescription or quitting my medication. He looked at me like I was being difficult. Said we should "just monitor it" and "see how it goes." Twenty years of watching my patients decline on these medications. Thirty-eight years in nursing. And his best advice was drink more water.

I sat in my car in the parking lot for ten minutes after that appointment. Just sat there. Staring at the steering wheel. I wasn't sad. I was angry. Because I've been a nurse long enough to know when a doctor is telling you he doesn't have an answer but doesn't want to say it. "Let's just monitor" is doctor for "I don't know what to do, and your problem isn't urgent enough for me to figure it out."

I wasn't about to just sit there and "monitor" while my body got worse.

So I just dealt with it. Miralax. Metamucil. Prune juice. Magnesium supplements. Bought a squatty potty. Nothing really worked, but what else was I supposed to do?

My sister found out I was spending money on supplements and natural remedies and told me I was "turning into one of those people." She said I should just listen to my doctor. Easy for her to say — she's not the one lying awake at night on day 8 wondering if she's going to end up in the ER. Not until May, when a doctor said one sentence to me that I should have been told in January.

By then it had already cost me the worst night of 24 years on that floor.

I haven't repeated any of this to a single person I work with. I'm about to put all of it on the internet with my name on it.

My name is Hannah. I'm 56 and I've been on the same med-surg floor since I was 32.

For 11 of those years I did the prep teaching for our GI lab. I'm the one who hands you the jug and tells you, kindly, that yes, you do have to drink all of it.

I added it up on a quiet night shift once, for no reason except that I was curious. 430 people I've handed that sheet to. Water. Fiber. Keep moving.

I believed every word of it. It's good advice.

It's the right advice for ordinary people. I didn't find out there's a group of us it's wrong for until I became one of them.

And when it goes bad on that floor, I'm the one they call. Everybody there knows it.

There's a rule about this in my profession. If something is going on with you that affects your ability to do your job, you report it. You don't sit at home and decide on your own that you're fine.

I didn't report it. And I'll tell you the honest reason, which isn't the one you'd guess. It wasn't the shame, although there was plenty of that.

It was that I knew the second I said it out loud, somebody was going to take my prescription away.

So. The medication.

I started last October, and I need to be clear about this next part.

The shot worked. 61 pounds. My A1c is the best it's been since I was 40. My knees stopped hurting on a 12 hour shift, which I'd quietly accepted was just what the rest of my life was going to feel like.

And the food noise stopped. I've never been able to explain that one to anybody who hasn't had it. It was there every waking minute since I was 15, and then it was gone.

I wasn't giving that up. Not for anything.

That's the whole reason this got as bad as it did.

I didn't know it that October, but I was already about six months out from the worst night of my career.

There's no day one with this. It comes on so slow that you never get a morning where you decide something is wrong.

By December I was sick most of the day.

I assumed that was the medication. Everybody assumes that's the medication. It's the famous one, it's on the label, and it's what my own doctor said when I brought it up.

I was wrong about that, and it took me until May to find out why. Hold onto it, because it's the part I most want somebody to read.

I also stopped going.

I'd gone every single morning of my adult life. Six ten in the morning, before work, 30 years, and I never once thought about it, which is the thing about a body that works. You don't notice it.

By December it was every second day. By January it was every fourth or fifth. Then I stopped being able to predict it at all, and I started keeping a number in my head. What day I was on. I didn't decide to do that. It was just always there, the way you always roughly know what time it is.

So in January I did the sensible thing. I want you to notice that I did the sensible thing, because of what it got me.

I told my doctor. I said it had been 6 days and that I was worried about it.

He didn't look up from the screen.

He said, "Are you drinking enough water? Try to get a little more fiber in there."

Then he said, "Now. Your A1c. This is wonderful."

That was the appointment.

I have an opinion about it. I've had 8 months to sit with it and I'm going to keep it professional. But I have one.

So I did what everybody does. I started buying.

Metamucil first, because that's what I'd just been told to do. When that did nothing I went to psyllium on its own. When that did nothing either I started on Miralax, a capful in my coffee every morning, because that's the only way I would get it down.

The Miralax worked for about 10 days. So I added magnesium at night. That worked for about a week. So I doubled it.

Then stool softeners, two with breakfast, on top of all of it.

Then prunes. Prune juice. Warm prune juice with butter melted into it, which is exactly as bad as it sounds.

And then the thing nobody wants to admit they've bought. Enemas, in a paper bag, from a pharmacy two towns over, because I didn't want to be seen buying them at the one by our house.

By March I was taking five things every single day just to stay level, with an extra dose on Sunday nights before my shot because Mondays were always the worst.

I was still going about once a week.

Every one of those things worked for a few days. Not one of them worked for a month.

And here's the part I've never said to anybody, because I know some of you are sitting in it right now.

I was doing the math. 61 pounds and the best bloodwork of my adult life, against not being able to go to the bathroom.

My husband asked me once, in March, standing at the sink.

Ray is a retired firefighter. 29 years married, and there's very little he hasn't seen or heard.

He said, "Are you okay? Because you are not okay."

I told him I was tired. I looked straight at him and lied about it, and he let it go because I asked him to.

Now April.

I had a patient in 412 who had come in at the start of the month. 80 years old. I'm changing his name, so let's call him Denny.

He called me boss. Every single time. "Morning, boss." He asked about my grandson by name and he got the name right, which almost nobody does, because it isn't a name people expect.

He was doing well. He was going home that week.

The night it happened I was on day 8 myself.

I want to be honest about what 8 days does, because I don't think people understand that it stops being about the bathroom. You're frightened. And I know what a bowel looks like when it's been left too long, because I've stood there and looked at the films. Knowing more didn't help me. It made it worse.

I went into the bathroom on four, past the chapel, at about two thirty, because it's the one nobody uses.

I was in there long enough that I'd stopped trying. I was sitting with my head against the wall, sweating, trying to figure out whether I was going to have to go somewhere myself and be the patient.

And then I heard it. You know the sound before you know what it is. The overhead, and then the running.

412.

I got up and my legs went and I sat back down.

I've gone over this more times than is good for me. It wasn't that I decided to stay. It was that I couldn't straighten up, and I couldn't get my clothes right, and I was shaking too bad to do either.

Tanya knocked on the door twice.

I didn't answer her.

By the time I got out there it was finished. They had him back. He was fine, or as fine as an 80 year old man is after that.

Four minutes. That's my own estimate. I've never checked it against the record because I don't want to know.

The next morning he called me boss.

And nobody said one word to me about that door. Not Tanya. Not anybody.

That's the part I didn't expect and haven't been able to put down since. There was no consequence. Nobody even asked. I got away with it completely, and I've found that far harder to live with than being caught.

I sat in my car in the staff lot before I drove home, and I cried for about 20 minutes. I haven't cried like that since my mother.

In May there was blood.

I can talk myself out of most things. I couldn't talk myself out of that.

So I let one of our GI docs get me on his schedule, and he scoped me in the middle of the month.

It came back clear. Nothing sinister.

Afterwards he sat down on the end of the gurney while I was still coming out of it, and he asked me what I'd been taking for it.

I listed it. All of it. It took a while.

He said, "None of that was ever going to work. Every one of those treats what's already in the pipe. Nobody's looking at the pipe."

I asked him what he meant.

"Bile. You only make it when there's food to break down. You're barely eating. So you're barely making any."

I said I still didn't see what that had to do with it.

"Because breaking food down isn't the only thing it does. It's what keeps the colon slick enough for anything to move through it. No bile, nothing's slick. It dries out and it stops."

Then I asked him about the sickness. The thing I'd been blaming on the shot since December.

He said, "That's not the drug. That's you being full. It's got nowhere to go but back up."

And then the sentence. The one I said at the top of this.

"And you've all been putting fiber on top of it. Which is like unblocking a toilet by pushing more paper down it."

Then he shrugged and went off to write it up, because to him this wasn't a revelation. It was a Tuesday.

I went home and sat on the edge of the bed with my coat still on.

Because it explained all of it. The prunes. The gallon of water I was tracking in an app. The paper bag from a pharmacy in another town. Five months of it, all aimed at the wrong end.

It also meant there was nothing in my bathroom cabinet that was ever going to help me. Every single one of those things is built to push from the bottom.

And then I worked out the second half of it, sitting there, and that was worse.

Because I did nothing about it for three weeks.

I want to be honest about that as well, because it's the strangest part of the whole thing. I knew exactly what was wrong with me. A man had just drawn me the diagram. And I still went to the pharmacy that Saturday and bought more Miralax, because it was the only thing on the shelf and I didn't know what else a person was supposed to do.

I got quietly worse.

Then Tanya.

First week of June, in the locker room, nobody else in there.

She said, "I knocked on that door in April."

I didn't say anything.

She said, "I knew what you were doing in there. Because it's what I do in there."

Tanya's been on Wegovy since last spring. We work three shifts a week together, and neither of us had said one word to the other one.

She had a bottle in her lunch bag. She said she'd been carrying it around for a week trying to figure out how to bring any of this up with me.

I'm the last woman alive who buys a supplement. I've spent 24 years watching people arrive on my floor with shopping bags full of bottles they saw on Facebook, and what's being sold to women on this medication right now is the worst of it. Half of it is the same fiber blend that was a prebiotic three years ago with GLP-1 printed on the front in a new font.

She said, "I know. Read the back of it before you tell me I've lost my mind."

So I stood there in my coat and read the back of it.

Omyo. I'd never heard of it. That didn't help.

14 things. Not one I had to look up, and not one I'd have flagged for a patient.

The first three were milk thistle, dandelion and beetroot.

Those are bile. All three of them.

That's the only reason I didn't hand it straight back to her. Not because I believed it. Because it was the only thing anybody had put in front of me that was aimed at the right end.

Then ginger and artichoke, which are for the squeeze. Your gut moves everything along by squeezing, and on this medication that slows way down with the rest of you. Slick on its own isn't enough. Something still has to push.

And nothing that forces anything. No senna. Nothing in there that was going to want a bigger dose out of me next month, which after five months of doubling everything was the part I stood there and read twice.

I still thought it was probably nothing. I'd spent about $400 that year on things that worked for a week, and I'd run out of ways to be hopeful about any of it.

But it was the only thing anybody had handed me that started at the top.

Two capsules before bed. I started it on a Tuesday.

I want to be honest about the first two days, because if you're the kind of person who gives something 48 hours before you decide it's another waste of money, you'd have thrown it out.

Nothing Tuesday. Nothing Wednesday.

Thursday morning I went, and it wasn't dramatic. It was just easy. No bracing myself, nothing taken alongside it, no 20 minutes.

I was still skeptical. It was one time.

Week one I went three times. I'd been going about once a week, so that number meant something to me that it won't mean to anybody else.

Week two I noticed my waistband before I noticed anything else. And I could breathe lying down, which I hadn't been able to do since February and had somehow decided was just how I slept now.

Week three the sickness stopped. I'd decided that was the price of the medication and that I was stuck with it for as long as I stayed on.

Week five I realized I didn't know what day I was on.

I'd carried that number every waking minute for five months. I didn't decide to stop. I noticed one morning, brushing my teeth, that it wasn't there, and I can't tell you when it went.

In July we had another one. A woman on the other side of the floor.

I heard the overhead and I stood up and I went, and I was the first one through that door.

I hadn't been sure I could still do that. I'd been carrying it around since April, quietly, that maybe I wasn't that person anymore.

Tanya saw me go. She's never said anything about it and she never will, and that's fine, because we both know.

Then there's Charlene.

Charlene is one of ours. I told her about it at the end of June, once I was sure it wasn't a fluke, and she said she'd order some. She meant it at the time. You know how that goes.

She switched to a different shot instead, because somebody told her it was better on that one. It followed her straight over. Of course it did.

She came off the medication altogether in July. She'd lost 30 pounds and her blood pressure was normal for the first time in 9 years.

She's put 19 of it back on since.

She said to me two weeks ago, "I wish I'd just ordered it when you told me."

That's the one I think about. Not my own bad nights. The women who did everything right, finally got the thing they'd been chasing half their lives, and handed it back over something that had a fix nobody had bothered to tell them about.

And I know what people say about April. He lived, so no harm done.

I don't find that comforting and I'm not going to pretend I do.

So here's why I'm putting my name on this.

If you used to go every single morning without ever thinking about it, and then it was every second day, and then it was every fourth, and now you couldn't tell me when it was.

If you're sick most of the day and you've been blaming the shot for it.

If you're taking three or four things every night just to stay level, and every one of them worked for a week and then it didn't.

If you have the paper bag from the pharmacy where nobody knows you.

If you've started quietly asking yourself whether all of this is worth it.

Then I'd like to save you the five months.

You're not failing at this. You were given the wrong instructions. Water and fiber is the right advice for ordinary constipation, and what happens to us on this medication isn't ordinary constipation. It starts at the top. Everything we were told to buy works at the bottom.

And you don't have to be standing in a hospital for this to be taking something from you. Most of what it takes, it takes quietly.

What I wanted back wasn't complicated. I wanted to stop thinking about it all day. I wanted to trust my own body again and get on with things.

Somebody's going to ask me for it, so I'll save us both the messages. https://omyohealth.com/products/glp1-digestive-support

I ordered three the second time around. Two for me, because I'd already figured out what happens if I run out and I wasn't willing to find that out twice.

The third one is still in my locker with Charlene's name on it. She won't take it now. There's nothing left for it to help with.

I told Ray last week. All of it, including April.

I haven't told my manager.

I guess this is how I'm telling her.

Denny went home four days after that night. He came past the desk on his way out and he told me I was the best one on that floor and he called me boss one more time.

I've never corrected him.

That's the woman I'd like to go on being, and for the first time since last winter I think I might be her again.

EDIT. I wasn't expecting any of this and my inbox is a disaster. I'm sorry to everyone I haven't gotten back to yet.

The same few questions keep coming up, so I'll just answer them here.

Yes, it's called Omyo, and the link is up above. A lot of you scrolled past it, so here it is again. https://omyohealth.com/products/glp1-digestive-support

Quite a few of you have said you're on the fence because you've been burned before. So have I. There's a money back guarantee on it, which is the only reason I was willing to spend anything at all after the year I'd had. Take it for a few weeks and if nothing happens for you, send it back.

On stock, I have nothing to do with the company and there's nothing I can do about that. All I can tell you is that when I reordered in August I waited 11 days, and that's exactly why I keep a spare in my locker now.

I'd gone every single morning of my adult life. Six ten in the morning, before work, 30 years, and I never once thought about it, which is the thing about a body that works. You don't notice it.

By December it was every second day. By January it was every fourth or fifth. Then I stopped being able to predict it at all, and I started keeping a number in my head. What day I was on. I didn't decide to do that. It was just always there, the way you always roughly know what time it is.

So in January I did the sensible thing. I want you to notice that I did the sensible thing, because of what it got me.

I told my doctor. I said it had been 6 days and that I was worried about it.

He didn't look up from the screen.

He said, "Are you drinking enough water? Try to get a little more fiber in there."

Then he said, "Now. Your A1c. This is wonderful."

That was the appointment.

I have an opinion about it. I've had 8 months to sit with it and I'm going to keep it professional. But I have one.

So I did what everybody does. I started buying.

Metamucil first, because that's what I'd just been told to do. When that did nothing I went to psyllium on its own. When that did nothing either I started on Miralax, a capful in my coffee every morning, because that's the only way I would get it down.

The Miralax worked for about 10 days. So I added magnesium at night. That worked for about a week. So I doubled it.

Then stool softeners, two with breakfast, on top of all of it.

Then prunes. Prune juice. Warm prune juice with butter melted into it, which is exactly as bad as it sounds.

And then the thing nobody wants to admit they've bought. Enemas, in a paper bag, from a pharmacy two towns over, because I didn't want to be seen buying them at the one by our house.

By March I was taking five things every single day just to stay level, with an extra dose on Sunday nights before my shot because Mondays were always the worst.

I was still going about once a week.

Every one of those things worked for a few days. Not one of them worked for a month.

And here's the part I've never said to anybody, because I know some of you are sitting in it right now.

I was doing the math. 61 pounds and the best bloodwork of my adult life, against not being able to go to the bathroom.

My husband asked me once, in March, standing at the sink.

Ray is a retired firefighter. 29 years married, and there's very little he hasn't seen or heard.

He said, "Are you okay? Because you are not okay."

I told him I was tired. I looked straight at him and lied about it, and he let it go because I asked him to.

Now April.

I had a patient in 412 who had come in at the start of the month. 80 years old. I'm changing his name, so let's call him Denny.

He called me boss. Every single time. "Morning, boss." He asked about my grandson by name and he got the name right, which almost nobody does, because it isn't a name people expect.

He was doing well. He was going home that week.

The night it happened I was on day 8 myself.

I want to be honest about what 8 days does, because I don't think people understand that it stops being about the bathroom. You're frightened. And I know what a bowel looks like when it's been left too long, because I've stood there and looked at the films. Knowing more didn't help me. It made it worse.

I went into the bathroom on four, past the chapel, at about two thirty, because it's the one nobody uses.

I was in there long enough that I'd stopped trying. I was sitting with my head against the wall, sweating, trying to figure out whether I was going to have to go somewhere myself and be the patient.

And then I heard it. You know the sound before you know what it is. The overhead, and then the running.

412.

I got up and my legs went and I sat back down.

I've gone over this more times than is good for me. It wasn't that I decided to stay. It was that I couldn't straighten up, and I couldn't get my clothes right, and I was shaking too bad to do either.

Tanya knocked on the door twice.

I didn't answer her.

By the time I got out there it was finished. They had him back. He was fine, or as fine as an 80 year old man is after that.

Four minutes. That's my own estimate. I've never checked it against the record because I don't want to know.

The next morning he called me boss.

And nobody said one word to me about that door. Not Tanya. Not anybody.

That's the part I didn't expect and haven't been able to put down since. There was no consequence. Nobody even asked. I got away with it completely, and I've found that far harder to live with than being caught.

I sat in my car in the staff lot before I drove home, and I cried for about 20 minutes. I haven't cried like that since my mother.

In May there was blood.

I can talk myself out of most things. I couldn't talk myself out of that.

So I let one of our GI docs get me on his schedule, and he scoped me in the middle of the month.

It came back clear. Nothing sinister.

Afterwards he sat down on the end of the gurney while I was still coming out of it, and he asked me what I'd been taking for it.

I listed it. All of it. It took a while.

He said, "None of that was ever going to work. Every one of those treats what's already in the pipe. Nobody's looking at the pipe."

I asked him what he meant.

"Bile. You only make it when there's food to break down. You're barely eating. So you're barely making any."

I said I still didn't see what that had to do with it.

"Because breaking food down isn't the only thing it does. It's what keeps the colon slick enough for anything to move through it. No bile, nothing's slick. It dries out and it stops."

Then I asked him about the sickness. The thing I'd been blaming on the shot since December.

He said, "That's not the drug. That's you being full. It's got nowhere to go but back up."

And then the sentence. The one I said at the top of this.

"And you've all been putting fiber on top of it. Which is like unblocking a toilet by pushing more paper down it."

Then he shrugged and went off to write it up, because to him this wasn't a revelation. It was a Tuesday.

I went home and sat on the edge of the bed with my coat still on.

Because it explained all of it. The prunes. The gallon of water I was tracking in an app. The paper bag from a pharmacy in another town. Five months of it, all aimed at the wrong end.

It also meant there was nothing in my bathroom cabinet that was ever going to help me. Every single one of those things is built to push from the bottom.

And then I worked out the second half of it, sitting there, and that was worse.

Because I did nothing about it for three weeks.

I want to be honest about that as well, because it's the strangest part of the whole thing. I knew exactly what was wrong with me. A man had just drawn me the diagram. And I still went to the pharmacy that Saturday and bought more Miralax, because it was the only thing on the shelf and I didn't know what else a person was supposed to do.

I got quietly worse.

Then Tanya.

First week of June, in the locker room, nobody else in there.

She said, "I knocked on that door in April."

I didn't say anything.

She said, "I knew what you were doing in there. Because it's what I do in there."

Tanya's been on Wegovy since last spring. We work three shifts a week together, and neither of us had said one word to the other one.

She had a bottle in her lunch bag. She said she'd been carrying it around for a week trying to figure out how to bring any of this up with me.

I'm the last woman alive who buys a supplement. I've spent 24 years watching people arrive on my floor with shopping bags full of bottles they saw on Facebook, and what's being sold to women on this medication right now is the worst of it. Half of it is the same fiber blend that was a prebiotic three years ago with GLP-1 printed on the front in a new font.

She said, "I know. Read the back of it before you tell me I've lost my mind."

So I stood there in my coat and read the back of it.

Omyo. I'd never heard of it. That didn't help.

14 things. Not one I had to look up, and not one I'd have flagged for a patient.

The first three were milk thistle, dandelion and beetroot.

Those are bile. All three of them.

That's the only reason I didn't hand it straight back to her. Not because I believed it. Because it was the only thing anybody had put in front of me that was aimed at the right end.

Then ginger and artichoke, which are for the squeeze. Your gut moves everything along by squeezing, and on this medication that slows way down with the rest of you. Slick on its own isn't enough. Something still has to push.

And nothing that forces anything. No senna. Nothing in there that was going to want a bigger dose out of me next month, which after five months of doubling everything was the part I stood there and read twice.

I still thought it was probably nothing. I'd spent about $400 that year on things that worked for a week, and I'd run out of ways to be hopeful about any of it.

But it was the only thing anybody had handed me that started at the top.

Two capsules before bed. I started it on a Tuesday.

I want to be honest about the first two days, because if you're the kind of person who gives something 48 hours before you decide it's another waste of money, you'd have thrown it out.

Nothing Tuesday. Nothing Wednesday.

Thursday morning I went, and it wasn't dramatic. It was just easy. No bracing myself, nothing taken alongside it, no 20 minutes.

I was still skeptical. It was one time.

Week one I went three times. I'd been going about once a week, so that number meant something to me that it won't mean to anybody else.

Week two I noticed my waistband before I noticed anything else. And I could breathe lying down, which I hadn't been able to do since February and had somehow decided was just how I slept now.

Week three the sickness stopped. I'd decided that was the price of the medication and that I was stuck with it for as long as I stayed on.

Week five I realized I didn't know what day I was on.

I'd carried that number every waking minute for five months. I didn't decide to stop. I noticed one morning, brushing my teeth, that it wasn't there, and I can't tell you when it went.

In July we had another one. A woman on the other side of the floor.

I heard the overhead and I stood up and I went, and I was the first one through that door.

I hadn't been sure I could still do that. I'd been carrying it around since April, quietly, that maybe I wasn't that person anymore.

Tanya saw me go. She's never said anything about it and she never will, and that's fine, because we both know.

Then there's Charlene.

Charlene is one of ours. I told her about it at the end of June, once I was sure it wasn't a fluke, and she said she'd order some. She meant it at the time. You know how that goes.

She switched to a different shot instead, because somebody told her it was better on that one. It followed her straight over. Of course it did.

She came off the medication altogether in July. She'd lost 30 pounds and her blood pressure was normal for the first time in 9 years.

She's put 19 of it back on since.

She said to me two weeks ago, "I wish I'd just ordered it when you told me."

That's the one I think about. Not my own bad nights. The women who did everything right, finally got the thing they'd been chasing half their lives, and handed it back over something that had a fix nobody had bothered to tell them about.

And I know what people say about April. He lived, so no harm done.

I don't find that comforting and I'm not going to pretend I do.

So here's why I'm putting my name on this.

If you used to go every single morning without ever thinking about it, and then it was every second day, and then it was every fourth, and now you couldn't tell me when it was.

If you're sick most of the day and you've been blaming the shot for it.

If you're taking three or four things every night just to stay level, and every one of them worked for a week and then it didn't.

If you have the paper bag from the pharmacy where nobody knows you.

If you've started quietly asking yourself whether all of this is worth it.

Then I'd like to save you the five months.

You're not failing at this. You were given the wrong instructions. Water and fiber is the right advice for ordinary constipation, and what happens to us on this medication isn't ordinary constipation. It starts at the top. Everything we were told to buy works at the bottom.

And you don't have to be standing in a hospital for this to be taking something from you. Most of what it takes, it takes quietly.

What I wanted back wasn't complicated. I wanted to stop thinking about it all day. I wanted to trust my own body again and get on with things.

Somebody's going to ask me for it, so I'll save us both the messages. https://omyohealth.com/products/glp1-digestive-support

I ordered three the second time around. Two for me, because I'd already figured out what happens if I run out and I wasn't willing to find that out twice.

The third one is still in my locker with Charlene's name on it. She won't take it now. There's nothing left for it to help with.

I told Ray last week. All of it, including April.

I haven't told my manager.

I guess this is how I'm telling her.

Denny went home four days after that night. He came past the desk on his way out and he told me I was the best one on that floor and he called me boss one more time.

I've never corrected him.

That's the woman I'd like to go on being, and for the first time since last winter I think I might be her again.

Pat Greene was supposed to direct the choir at our church's hundredth anniversary celebration in October.

She had been preparing the program for two years. Twelve special selections. A full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta. Three guest soloists, including the granddaughter of our founding pastor flown in from Houston. Eight hundred people in the sanctuary. The Bishop of the Sixth Episcopal District. Two news crews from Channel 11 and Channel 5.

Pat sat in the back pew of the church she has served for twenty-two years, behind the third pillar on the left side where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to her twenty-eight-year-old assistant Roxanne Holcomb conduct her choir.

Pat had quit her Mounjaro® in February.

I'm going to say something most of us on these GLP-1 medications do not want to hear, and I'm not going to soften it because Pat did not get a soft version of this either.

Another bottle of fiber is not going to save your shots.

Not Miralax. Not Metamucil. Not the ninety-four-dollar prescription bulk-former your gastroenterologist called in last Thursday. Not the magnesium your daughter ordered for you off Amazon for forty-six dollars. Not the prune juice your mama swore by. Not the Smooth Move tea from the health food store in East Point.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I tried all of it for eleven months. And nine weeks ago I had a discontinuation appointment on the calendar for a Friday afternoon at one because I was done — done planning every Sunday morning around whether I could make it through service without leaving the sanctuary, done burping behind my hand at the Mothers Board meeting, done watching my own grandbabies and falling asleep on the couch while they watched cartoons at three in the afternoon.

I was going to walk into my prescriber's office at one o'clock, quit my Ozempic, and accept that I would be back to two hundred and thirty-four pounds within nine months. Maybe sooner. I had done it once before, after Marcus.

I almost let it happen. I was still listening to the same garbage that took my best friend's place at the piano.

Read every word of this. The answer is in here and it is not what your doctor told you.

My name is Gloria Mason. I'm 67. I live in Stone Mountain, Georgia — twenty minutes east of Atlanta — in the brick ranch house Marcus and I bought in 1989 with the down payment we saved for six years. Marcus passed eighteen months ago — September of '24, sudden heart attack at seventy-one, the morning after our forty-fifth anniversary dinner. He was retired from Aflac, he was a deacon at our church, and he was the only man I ever loved.

I have two grown daughters — Kendra in Tucker, Tracey in Decatur — and three grandchildren who keep me alive. I retired from Atlanta Public Schools in 2022 after thirty-two years as a guidance counselor, the last seventeen at Frederick Douglass High. I am active at Greater Mt. Zion AME Church, where Marcus and I were members for thirty-six years, and where I sit on the Mothers Board with eleven other women who have known me longer than my own daughters have.

In the nine months after Marcus passed, I ate. Not from hunger. From wanting something to do with my hands at seven in the morning when the house was too quiet. I gained fifty-six pounds. By June of last year I weighed two hundred and thirty-four — the most I had ever weighed in my life. My doctor told me my blood pressure was a hundred and sixty over a hundred and that we had two paths in front of us. I chose Ozempic®.

I started in July. By December I was down to one eighty-six. My pressure was normal. I had started walking on the trail at Stone Mountain Park three mornings a week. I had bought a dress at Phipps Plaza I had not had the courage to try on in twelve years.

I should have been thanking the Lord. The woman in the photograph on my dresser and the woman in my mirror were starting to match again.

Instead, I was sixty-seven years old, sitting in the back pew at Sunday morning service holding a folded handkerchief over my mouth because I had not gone normally in nine days and I could feel a sulphur burp coming up.

The constipation started in week four. By month three I was going every six or seven days, and only after a long fight. By month six the fight had stopped working.

The sulphur burps started in April. The kind that come up without warning. The kind that came up standing next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service. The kind I had never had in sixty-seven years of life. I started carrying breath mints in my pocketbook in a way I had not since I quit smoking in 1989.

The fatigue is what would have taken me. I am a sixty-seven-year-old woman with three grandbabies between two daughters who both work outside the home. I am the standing Tuesday and Thursday daycare. By July of last year I was driving to Kendra's house at two in the afternoon and falling asleep on the family-room couch while my eight-year-old grandson Caleb built Legos beside me on the floor. He told his mother. Kendra called me that night. She did not say it, but she was afraid.

And the brain fog. I lost the name of my own granddaughter Aniyah at the Mothers Board meeting in August. Just for fifteen seconds. I covered it. The two women across the table who noticed pretended they did not. I went out to my car in the church parking lot afterward and cried for ten minutes before I could drive home.

I told my prescriber.

"It happens with these medications, Mrs. Mason. Drink water. Try Miralax. Give it more time."

I tried what he said. I tried what Sister Carolyn from the Mothers Board suggested. I tried what my daughter Tracey saw on TikTok. By August I had been to the bathroom five times in three weeks.

I am a retired guidance counselor. I track things. Between February and August I spent five hundred and twenty dollars on supplements and laxatives. Miralax morning and night. Citrucel at lunch. Metamucil at dinner. A magnesium from the GNC at Camp Creek. A probiotic my daughter Tracey ordered from Amazon for forty-eight dollars. A prescription bulk-former my gastroenterologist wrote at ninety-four dollars out of pocket. Prune juice. Senna tea. A bottle of Smooth Move from a health-food store in East Point.

I had a basket of all of it in my pantry. Tracey saw it when she came over to drop off the grandbabies on a Sunday afternoon. She asked me what was happening. I told her I was fine.

I still had not gone normally in eight weeks. The sulphur burps were keeping me from communion on First Sundays. And meanwhile, my best friend Patricia was disappearing from the only thing she had ever loved more than us.

Patricia Anne Greene and I have been friends since 1968. We were both twelve years old, both in Sister Mae Hudson's youth choir at Greater Mt. Zion, both not very good singers if I am being honest with you. Pat had a voice like clear water by the time she was sixteen. I had a voice that does not need to be discussed further. Pat went on to study music education at Spelman College from '76 to '80, came back to our church in 1985, and was made music minister in 2003. She has been the music minister at Greater Mt. Zion for twenty-two years.

Our congregation does not have a Sunday service without Pat at that piano. Pat has not had a Sunday morning without our congregation since 1985. Marcus called her the heartbeat of our church right up until the day he passed.

She started Mounjaro® a year before I started Ozempic — same kind of grief story, different husband, hers passed in 2021. She lost fifty-one pounds. By December of '24 she was running again — she had been a sprinter at Spelman, I do not know if I told you that — and she was three months into rehearsals for the church's hundredth anniversary celebration scheduled for October. The committee had been planning it for two years. Pat was going to direct twelve special selections, a full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta, three guest soloists, and a praise dance from the youth ministry. Bishop Brown was coming from Washington. Two news crews.

In February she had a constipation streak that went fourteen days. She did not tell me. She did not tell her son Marcus Junior up in Athens. She filled out her own discontinuation paperwork on a Saturday night when she was alone in her kitchen. She quit her shots that week.

By May she had gained back twenty-three pounds. By July she had stopped coming to choir rehearsal — sent Roxanne in her place. By September she was up forty-six pounds. The depression came in heavy by the third week of September. She missed three Sundays in a row. People were calling me asking if Pat was all right. I did not know what to say.

The hundredth anniversary celebration was Sunday morning, October the twenty-first. The sanctuary was full. The Bishop preached for fifty-two minutes. Roxanne stood at Pat's piano and conducted Pat's program. Roxanne is twenty-eight years old. She is a very gifted young woman, the granddaughter of one of Pat's choir mothers from the eighties. She did her best.

Pat sat in the back pew on the left side, behind the third pillar where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to twenty-two years of her work being conducted by a young woman who had not yet been born when Pat first sat down at that piano.

After the service I went looking for her. Her car was already gone.

The next morning the church board met. By Wednesday word had spread that they were discussing transitioning Pat to "Music Minister Emeritus" — a respectful title for a forced retirement none of us thought we would see. Roxanne would take over permanently in January.

I drove home from running errands on Tuesday afternoon and sat in my car in my own driveway for thirty-five minutes before I could go inside. I called my prescriber's office and scheduled the discontinuation appointment for Friday at one. I did not tell my daughters. I did not tell anyone.

The next Wednesday was my regular Bible study night at the church. Wednesday evening women's Bible study, six-thirty to eight, the same group of women I have been studying scripture with for sixteen years. I had not been the last four Wednesdays. I had been telling myself I would skip another one and stay home in front of the television.

I do not skip Bible study. I made myself go.

After the lesson ended at eight, the women's group cleaned up together — folding chairs, clearing coffee cups from the church's silver urns, wiping down the folding tables in the fellowship hall. There were six of us at the start of the cleanup. Most of the others had already gone home by the time I was folding the last three chairs.

Doreen Williams came back from the kitchen with a trash bag in her hand.

Doreen is seventy-two. She is one of the matriarchs of our church and a fellow Mothers Board member. She was the lead pharmacist at the Greene Brothers Pharmacy on Cascade Road in southwest Atlanta from 1981 until they closed in 2019 — thirty-eight years filling prescriptions for half the Black families on the southside of this city. She was Marcus's friend before she was mine. She and her husband John were at his funeral.

She set the trash bag down. She looked at me across the folding table.

"Gloria. Sister. You sit down. We need to talk before you drive yourself home."

I sat down.

I told her everything in about twelve minutes. The constipation. The burps in the receiving line. Pat. The discontinuation appointment Friday at one. I cried in the fellowship hall of the church Marcus and I had served for thirty-six years for the first time since the morning he passed.

Doreen handed me a clean napkin with the church's name printed at the corner from the stack on the table. Then she sat down across from me and folded her hands the way she used to do when she was about to explain to me what a new prescription would do to my husband's pressure.

"Sister Gloria. Can I tell you what I learned in thirty-eight years filling prescriptions at Greene Brothers?"

"Please."

"These medications — Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro — slow your gastric emptying by fifty percent or more. That is how they make you feel full. That is how you got down to one eighty-six."

"I know that part."

"But here is what your prescriber did not tell you. When your stomach empties at half-speed, two things happen they do not put on the patient handout. First, food sits in your stomach long enough to ferment. Bacteria break down food that should have moved on six hours ago. That is where the sulphur burps come from. Second, the slowdown runs all the way through your gut. Stool sits longer. Dries. Compacts. By the time it reaches your colon, the muscle contractions your body normally uses to push it out are not strong enough to compensate."

"That is the constipation."

"That is the constipation. Now let me tell you what the supplement industry has been doing to women like us for the last two years."

"Tell me."

"Fiber works by adding bulk that needs gut motility — muscle contractions — to push it through. But your medication is intentionally suppressing those contractions. When you add fiber on a GLP-1, you are adding bulk that has nowhere to go. You are not relieving constipation. You are making the bloating worse."

I thought about every morning of forced Citrucel water I drank at the kitchen sink before I drove to Tuesday daycare at Kendra's.

"Stimulant laxatives — Dulcolax, Senna, Smooth Move — they force the intestinal muscles to contract. But your medication is suppressing those exact contractions. The two drugs fight each other inside your gut. The GLP-1 wins almost every time. That is why you have been cramping at three in the morning and still not going."

I thought about the night in August when I had taken three Senna tablets and missed the next morning's Mothers Board breakfast for the first time in nine years.

"What works?"

"You need an osmotic mechanism. Magnesium pulls water into your colon without requiring muscle contractions. That is the correct approach for a slowed system. But the dose has to be right, and most of what is on the shelf at the GNC or on Amazon is not the dose on the label."

"What else?"

"You need a prokinetic — something that speeds your gastric emptying enough to stop the fermentation, but does not fight the medication. There is exactly one botanical that does this reliably. Ginger root extract, at a specific dose and gingerol standardization. The supplement industry has been selling unstandardized ginger powder under premium labels for years. Most of it has no measurable active compound at all."

"How do you know?"

"My daughter Renee works at a contract testing lab in Norcross. She runs assays on commercial supplements when one company is suing another for label fraud. Last year she ran a panel on twelve GLP-1-positioned supplements being sold to women like you and me. Nine were underdosed on magnesium. Five had no measurable gingerols. Two contained heavy metals above CFR-111 limits. One was three percent of the magnesium it claimed on the label."

"How many passed?"

"One. Just one."

She wrote a name on the back of the Bible study handout, where the verse memorization section had been left blank.

"GLP-1 SOS™. Started by a woman who was on Wegovy and went through what you are going through. She found a real formulator and got it right. I have told every Mother on this board who is on these medications. I have told the deaconess at Big Bethel. I have no business relationship with the company. I just do not want any more Pats."

I looked at the handout. GLP-1 SOS™ written in Doreen's careful pharmacist's print. Then I looked at her.

"Will this work for Pat?"

"It will work for Pat if she will take it. Right now, you. Two capsules with dinner. The magnesium pulls water in gently overnight. The ginger speeds your stomach emptying. Regularity inside three or four days. Sulphur burps usually gone within forty-eight hours. Energy back in the second or third week as the B12 builds up."

I cancelled the discontinuation appointment from the church parking lot before I drove home. I ordered GLP-1 SOS™ from glp1sos.com that night at the kitchen table where Marcus and I had taken every meal of our marriage.

Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing. Day three, I went, in my own bathroom, gently, at six fifty AM. No cramping. No straining. Just normal.

I sat on the edge of the tub for a minute afterward and let myself believe it.

Forty-eight hours after my first dose, I stood next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service and shook the hands of about a hundred and forty members of my congregation without covering my mouth with a handkerchief once.

Week two, I slept through the night for the first time since March.

Week three, I had energy at three in the afternoon for the first time since the spring.

Week four, I kept the grandbabies on a Tuesday and a Thursday and on Saturday I drove down to Athens for the afternoon to visit Kendra's mother-in-law at her assisted living facility. I did not fall asleep once.

I am still on Ozempic®. Down to one eighty-two. My blood pressure last visit was one twenty-eight over seventy-six. My doctor said it is the best she has seen on me in twenty years.

That was eight weeks ago. Haven't been constipated since. Haven't had a sulphur burp since.

Every time I see Pat — who is back on Mounjaro now and four weeks into her own bottle of GLP-1 SOS™ — I think about her sitting behind the third pillar. The church board has agreed to delay any Emeritus decision until February. Pat is going to direct the Christmas concert on December the fifteenth. Roxanne will play the offertory. Something is happening inside the gut of every person on a GLP-1 medication right now.

It's not on the side effect list. It's not in the clinical trials. And your prescribing doctor — who is almost certainly not a gastroenterologist — has no idea it's coming.

My name is Dr. Rachel Scott. I'm a gastroenterologist. And I do.

I want to tell you about the morning I stood in my own bathroom, six weeks into a medication I had personally prescribed to dozens of patients, and realized I had no idea what was happening inside my own gut.

I'm a gastroenterologist. I have been for 11 years. I specialize in motility disorders — the conditions where the digestive system stops moving the way it's supposed to. I know this system better than almost anyone.

And I was standing there, stomach already visibly distended before I had eaten a single thing, completely stumped.

That's where this story starts. Not in my clinic. In my bathroom at 6am.

Eight months ago I started Mounjaro.

My PCP and I had discussed it. I understood the mechanism — I'm a GI specialist, I had read the clinical data, I had watched the trials come out in real time. I knew it slowed gastric emptying. I had warned my own patients about constipation. I thought I knew exactly what I was walking into.

The first five weeks were fine. Appetite down. Some nausea on injection days. Nothing I hadn't expected.

Then week six arrived.

I woke up one Tuesday morning and my stomach was already distended. Not the kind of bloating that comes from dinner the night before. Already there. Before coffee. Before breakfast. Before anything. I pressed my hand against my abdomen and felt the tightness that shouldn't have been there.

I told myself it was nothing.

By noon it was worse.

By 3pm I looked — I want to be precise here, because precision matters in medicine — like I was in my second trimester.

I had eaten four bites of yogurt and half a piece of toast that day. The medication had done exactly what it was supposed to do — I had no appetite. And yet standing in the hospital bathroom between patient appointments, looking at myself in the mirror, I looked like someone who had eaten an enormous meal.

I was losing weight on the scale. I was more bloated than I had been in a decade.

The irony was not something I could ignore for long.

I did what I tell patients to do.

I added a high-quality probiotic. Increased my water intake to three liters a day. Started magnesium glycinate at night. Cut all dairy. Kept a food diary for three weeks — every meal, every symptom, every time of day the distension was worse.

I tracked. I restricted. I supplemented. I did everything right.

Nothing changed.

Week eight. Still distended every morning. Still looking visibly pregnant by afternoon. A colleague stopped me in the hallway one afternoon and asked, quietly, if everything was okay. She was looking at my stomach. I said yes and kept walking. I got to the elevator and stood there, doors closed, alone, and felt something I had not felt in a very long time.

Completely lost in my own body.

I am not someone who gets lost. I have 11 years of training. I have diagnosed this exact problem in hundreds of patients. I have sat across from people describing these exact symptoms and explained to them, calmly and clearly, what was happening and what to do about it.

And I could not apply that knowledge to myself.

That was the night I sat down and actually started reading.

Not patient handouts. Not clinical guidelines. The actual research. The studies I assign to residents. The mechanisms I teach in a classroom. And about two hours in, reading a 2019 paper on GLP-1 receptor agonists and gastrointestinal motility, I stopped.

Read the same paragraph three times.

Set the paper down.

Because in 11 years of gastroenterology, I had never fully connected these two things in the way I was connecting them right now. Not about myself. Not about my patients. Not about what was actually happening inside the gut of every person on one of these medications.

Here is what I had been missing.

Your small intestine has a cleaning cycle.

Between meals — when your stomach is empty and you are not actively digesting anything — your gut runs a rhythmic sweeping wave. Roughly every 90 minutes. Starting near the stomach, moving all the way through to your colon. Gastroenterologists call it the Migrating Motor Complex. The MMC.

Its job is simple. Push everything downward. Bacteria, debris, anything that doesn't belong in the small intestine — swept down toward the colon where it can be eliminated. In a healthy gut, this wave runs like clockwork. You never feel it. You never think about it. It just runs.

And it is the single most important mechanism keeping your small intestine clean.

Now here is what GLP-1 medications do that nobody talks about.

They slow gastric motility on purpose. That's part of the mechanism — slower emptying means food sits longer in your stomach, you feel full faster, you eat less, you lose weight. Intended. By design.

But the MMC is part of the same motility system.

When GLP-1 medications slow your gut down, the MMC slows down too.

The sweeping wave becomes weak. Infrequent. In some patients it stops running altogether.

And when that cleaning cycle stops, bacteria that should be swept down toward the colon start accumulating in the small intestine. They colonize the lining. They ferment whatever passes through — not specific trigger foods, not things you could eliminate by changing your diet — anything. They produce gas. They inflame the intestinal wall. They damage the lining over time.

The condition has a name. Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth. SIBO.

And I had it.

Not because of anything I ate. Not because of anything I did wrong. Because the medication I was on had suppressed the cleaning cycle in my small intestine and bacteria had accumulated in the space the wave was no longer clearing.

I sat at my desk at 11pm reading this and felt two things at once.

The first was relief. Because I finally understood what was happening to me.

The second was something harder to name. Because I had been prescribing this medication to patients. And I had never once warned them about this.

I closed my laptop and went to bed. I didn't sleep well.

The next morning I started looking for what actually fixes this.

And here is where I need to be honest about something that took me longer to accept than it should have.

Probiotics don't fix this.

I know that. I teach that. Probiotics add bacteria to the gut. They do not stimulate the MMC. They do not restart the sweeping wave. Adding more bacteria to a small intestine that isn't clearing bacteria is not a solution. It might make things worse.

Magnesium softens stool. It does not restore motility.

Dietary restriction — cutting dairy, cutting gluten, eating plainer and plainer — reduces what the accumulated bacteria have to ferment. So you feel slightly less bloated. But the bacteria are still there. The wave is still stopped. The moment you eat anything, they ferment it and the bloating returns.

I had spent six weeks doing all three.

Treating the noise. Not the mechanism.

The only thing that restarts the MMC is a prokinetic stimulus. A compound that physically signals the gut wall to begin its sweeping wave again. I went looking for what the research actually supported.

The first thing I found was ginger root extract.

Not ginger tea. Not a generic ginger supplement. Ginger root extract standardized to 20% gingerols — the specific active compound that actually does something measurable. There is a randomized controlled trial showing standardized ginger extract directly increases MMC activity in patients with motility disorders. The mechanism is physical. Gingerols bind to receptors in the gut wall that trigger the sweeping wave to fire.

It tells the gut to move again. Directly.

Then artichoke leaf extract. Artichoke stimulates bile flow — and bile is a natural signaling molecule that triggers gut contractions. When bile moves properly, transit speeds up. Multiple placebo-controlled trials show artichoke leaf extract reduces bloating by over 40% in eight weeks in patients with functional digestive issues. Not a trend. A clinically meaningful reduction from published data.

Then berberine HCl. Berberine has been in gastroenterology research for years and I had never given it the attention it deserved. What it does specifically — and this distinction is critical — is reduce pathogenic bacterial overgrowth selectively. It targets the bacteria that accumulated in the small intestine while the MMC was suppressed, without wiping out the beneficial strains the way antibiotics do. Antibiotics take everything. Berberine is targeted.

And then the compound I had been systematically underweighting in my own patient recommendations for years.

CoreBiome Tributyrin.

Tributyrin is a stable, bioavailable form of butyrate — the short-chain fatty acid that is the primary fuel source for the cells lining your small intestine. When bacterial overgrowth runs in the small intestine for weeks or months, the lining takes real damage. Permeability increases. Inflammation compounds. And even after you restart the MMC and rebalance the bacteria, a damaged lining keeps producing symptoms.

Butyrate rebuilds it.

Without it, you can do everything else right and still feel terrible. Because the structural damage is still there.

It is the piece almost every gut protocol skips. Including the protocols I had been building for my own patients.

I spent three days sourcing all four compounds separately. Different companies. Different websites. One from a compounding pharmacy in another state. Trying to find the right standardization on each one, the right dose, the right form.

By the time I had everything I needed I had spent $340. And I wasn't even certain the doses were right.

I started taking them together the following Monday.

Week one. Honestly — nothing noticeable. Day four I thought I felt something. I didn't trust it.

Week two. The morning distension was lighter. Still there, but lighter. On day eleven I woke up and my stomach was flat when I got out of bed. I lay there for a moment and realized I had noticed it because I almost hadn't — the absence of something I had stopped expecting to be absent.

That's how you know something real is happening. Not a dramatic shift. The quiet disappearance of a thing you had accepted as permanent.

Week three. The afternoon distension — gone. Digestion felt complete. Food moved through. That stuck, heavy, still-full-from-a-meal-I-barely-ate feeling lifted entirely.

Week six. I ran a hydrogen breath test on myself. Hydrogen levels in the breath measure bacterial fermentation in the small intestine — elevated hydrogen means bacteria are active where they shouldn't be.

My result: 7 parts per million. Normal is under 10.

Six weeks earlier I had been symptomatic enough to have put money on a strongly positive result.

The bacteria were back in normal range. The MMC was running. The lining — I could feel it the way you feel the lifting of chronic low-grade inflammation, like a sound you'd stopped hearing going suddenly quiet — was recovering.

I kept going another six weeks to confirm. Twelve weeks total.

Then I walked into my clinic and did something I had never done before in 11 years of practice.

I started warning patients before their symptoms started.

The first patient I told was a woman named Linda. 54 years old. Had been on Ozempic for seven weeks. Coming in for an unrelated issue. No gut complaints yet.

I pulled her chart. Ozempic. Seven weeks. I thought about week six of Mounjaro. About the Tuesday morning bathroom. About standing in the elevator alone.

I told her what her prescribing doctor hadn't told her. That the medication she was on suppresses the cleaning wave in her small intestine. That bacteria accumulate predictably when that wave stops running. That this is not random or mysterious — it is a downstream consequence of the mechanism, and it is coming for most people on these drugs if they don't actively support their gut motility.

She looked at me the way patients look at you when they feel like someone finally told them something true.

"Why didn't my doctor tell me this?"

I didn't have a good answer for that.

What I did have was what I was taking. And I told her about it.

But here is what I couldn't keep doing — sending patients to source four separate compounds the way I had. Different websites. Uncertain standardization. $300 to $400 a month minimum if they did it right. Most people wouldn't do it right. Most people would buy one thing, get incomplete results, and conclude that nothing works.

Liquid drops absorb the moment they contact your mucous membranes. Faster to the bloodstream. Faster to the gut tissue that needs them.

Days seven to ten: Morning bloating starts to ease. The distension that was already there when you opened your eyes — lighter. The MMC is beginning to fire again, weakly at first, but firing.

Week six to eight: This is where most of my patients describe the real shift. The bloating that had become background noise — that they had started to accept as just how their body works now — quiets. Several patients have used the same words. They say their gut feels like it woke up.

Week twelve: This is when I retest. And consistently — not in every single patient, but consistently — what I find is bacterial populations back in normal range. Motility restored. Lining markers improved.

I'm a scientist. I don't make promises I cannot back with data.

What I will tell you with complete confidence is this.

If you are on a GLP-1 medication and your gut has gone sideways — if you are bloated in a way that makes no sense given what you are eating, if you are distended when you wake up, if fiber and magnesium and probiotics are not touching it — it is not random.
